newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss Jews fear anti-Semitism mounts in funds row.
newsitem.headline: Swiss Jews fear anti-Semitism mounts in funds row.

text.p: A leading Swiss Jew said on Monday that anti-Semitism was on the rise, fuelled by a government minister's accusation that Jewish groups seeking compensation for wartime suffering were trying to "blackmail" Switzerland.

Anti-Jewish feeling, long suppressed in Swiss society, is surfacing in letters and telephone calls to Jewish groups and virulent letters to newspapers, said Martin Rosenfeld, general secretary of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG).

He pinned the blame squarely on Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who Rosenfeld said had made such sentiment respectable last month by dismissing Jewish groups' calls for quick compensation as "extortion and blackmail".

"The whole thing arose after the comments from Delamuraz and the subsequent uproar. It had been quiet before," said Rosenfeld, whose organisation is an umbrella group for the roughly 30,000-strong Jewish community in Switzerland.

"There is clearly a connection. Many feel justified by Delamuraz, and also have the feeling that if a cabinet member is allowed to express himself this way, then the threshhold of anti-Semitism has been lowered."

Most of the mail comes from older people who object to Jewish calls for compensation 50 years after a war that neutral, democratic Switzerland did its best to stay out of -- even at the price of close economic collaboration with the Nazis.
"But there are also letters, only some of them anonymous, that contain clear or even crass comments," he said.

Many Swiss have rallied behind Delamuraz, whose comments as he finished a one-year term in the Swiss rotating presidency raised hackles at home and abroad and triggered threats that Jewish groups could call a boycott of Swiss banks next month.

One recent survey showed less than a third of Swiss surveyed thought the government should distance itself from Delamuraz. Another found 80 percent of respondents did not think Delamuraz should resign.

Rosenfeld said many letter-writers were showing a misplaced sense of solidarity with Switzerland by defending Delamuraz, who has said he regrets his comments may have offended Holocaust survivors and their families but has refused to apologise.

"It is not the case that the Swiss are especially anti-Semitic. There was always a latent anti-Semitism, but until now people did not dare to express it openly," he said, adding it was a clear but vocal minority that was now speaking out.

"The Jews want to see money from Switzerland," one person wrote to the conservative Neue Zuercher Zeitung daily. "Nothing other than money, money, money...If peace with the Palestinians made money, then the Jews would have forced it by now."
Leading newspapers have decried the development.

"When I hear Minister Delamuraz and his many friends, it sounds as if this were from the Middle Ages: The Jew who claims his basic rights is tiresome and 'extortionist'," a commentator for the liberal Tages-Anzeiger wrote at the weekend.

"The Jew should not be so brazen, but rather remain nice even if Switzerland still hesitates after half a century to own up to its long-established failures and compensate via a fund what still can be compensated," it added.

"With his stupid words, Delamuraz broke a taboo. He accused Jewish organisations of indecent behaviour. That was a signal and now old prejudices about Jews are breaking out again openly," SonntagsZeitung editor-in-chief Ueli Haldimann wrote.
"Not just among neo-Nazis. Latent Anti-Jewish feeling is still present, especially among the older population."
